speaker: Unknown
en: You've worked with many very high performing founder CEOs.
zh: 你与许多非常高效的创始人 CEO 共事过。

speaker: Unknown
en: Zuck, Cheryl Sandberg.
zh: Zuck，Cheryl Sandberg。

speaker: Unknown
en: Larry and Sergei at Google.
zh: Google 的 Larry 和 Sergei。

speaker: Unknown
en: Brett Taylor.
zh: Brett Taylor。

speaker: Unknown
en: Google, when I was there, felt like two PhD students paradise.
zh: Google，当我在那里的时候，感觉就像两个博士生的天堂。

speaker: Unknown
en: Facebook felt like 19-year-old hacker's dorm room.
zh: Facebook 感觉就像 19 岁黑客的宿舍。

speaker: Unknown
en: 80% of the culture of a company is literally defined by the personality of the founder.
zh: 公司 80% 的文化实际上是由创始人的个性定义的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Our job as operators or as leaders is to help articulate the culture that they're creating.
zh: 我们作为运营者或作为领导者的工作，是帮助阐明他们正在创造的文化。

speaker: Unknown
en: When a lot of people think Molly Graham, a lot of people think of giving away your Legos.
zh: 当很多人想到 Molly Graham 时，很多人会想到交出你的乐高。

speaker: Unknown
en: You have to grow as fast as your company is growing if you really want to take advantage, both learning to give away what you've gotten good at and move on to the next shiny pile of Legos.
zh: 你的成长速度必须和你的公司一样快，如果你真的想利用这一点的话，既要学会交出你擅长的东西，然后转移到下一堆闪亮的乐高积木。

speaker: Unknown
en: Sarah Caldwell.
zh: Sarah Caldwell。

speaker: Unknown
en: She told me that the framework that helped her most in her career is something that you call the J-curve versus stairs.
zh: 她告诉我，对她职业生涯帮助最大的框架是你称之为 J 曲线与楼梯的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: So Chamath, when he pitched me on this job, actually drew me a picture on a whiteboard.
zh: 所以 Chamath，当他向我推销这份工作时，实际上在白板上给我画了一张图。

speaker: Unknown
en: He said, the way a lot of people do careers is a set of stairs.
zh: 他说，很多人做职业的方式是一组楼梯。

speaker: Unknown
en: Just walk up the stairs and you'll get promoted every two years.
zh: 只要走上楼梯，你每两年就会升职。

speaker: Unknown
en: But that is boring.
zh: 但那很无聊。

speaker: Unknown
en: The much more fun careers are like jumping off cliffs and you do fall, but then you climb out way beyond where the stairs could ever get you.
zh: 更有趣的职业就像跳下悬崖，你确实会掉下去，但随后你爬出来的地方远远超过楼梯能带你去的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: Today, my guest is Molly Graham.
zh: 今天，我的嘉宾是 Molly Graham。

speaker: Unknown
en: Molly was an early employee at Google, also at Facebook, where she worked closely with Zuck on building the Chan Zuckerberg initiative.
zh: Molly 是 Google 的早期员工，也是 Facebook 的，她在那里与 Zuck 紧密合作建立了 Chan Zuckerberg initiative。

speaker: Unknown
en: She also worked with Brett Taylor on scaling Quip, which he sold to Salesforce.
zh: 她还与 Brett Taylor 合作扩展 Quip，他把它卖给了 Salesforce。

speaker: Unknown
en: She's also worked with hundreds of companies and founders helping them grow into the leaders that they want to become.
zh: 她还与数百家公司和创始人合作，帮助他们成长为想要成为的领导者。

speaker: Unknown
en: Today, she leads Glue Club, which is a community for leaders operating in changing, growing environments who want to develop themselves as quickly as their companies.
zh: 如今，她领导 Glue Club，这是一个为在变化、成长的环境中运营并希望与公司一样快速自我发展的领导者服务的社区。

speaker: Unknown
en: Molly is maybe most known for her advice to give away your Legos, which we chat about.
zh: Molly 也许最出名的建议是交出你的乐高，我们聊到了这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: Along with basically all of her favorite frameworks and mindsets and pieces of advice that she's developed and collected over time.
zh: 以及基本上所有她最喜欢的框架、心态和她随时间开发及收集的建议。

speaker: Unknown
en: For leaders who are going through rapid scale and growth and are just struggling to keep up.
zh: 对于那些正在经历快速扩张和增长并且正在努力跟上步伐的领导者。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think of this episode as a high growth handbook for leaders who are experiencing rapid scale.
zh: 我把这期节目视为一本为经历快速扩张的领导者准备的高增长手册。

speaker: Unknown
en: We cover the J curves versus stairs approach to career growth, the waterline model, and why you want to snorkel before you scuba.
zh: 我们涵盖了 J 曲线与楼梯的职业增长方法、水线模型，以及为什么你想在深潜之前先浮潜。

speaker: Unknown
en: Her six rules for creating goals and building alignment, her rules of thumb for dealing with rapid scale and lots of change.
zh: 她关于制定目标和建立一致性的六条规则，她应对快速扩张和大量变化的经验法则。

speaker: Unknown
en: The biggest lessons she's learned from Zuck and Sergei and Larry and Cheryl and Brett Taylor and so much more.
zh: 她从 Zuck 和 Sergei、Larry、Cheryl 和 Brett Taylor 那里学到的最大教训以及更多。

speaker: Unknown
en: Molly is incredible and you will be a better leader after listening to this episode.
zh: Molly 非常棒，听完这期节目后你会成为更好的领导者。

speaker: Unknown
en: A huge thank you to Eric Antonow, Ashley Murphy and Sarah Caldwell for suggesting topics and questions for this conversation.
zh: 非常感谢 Eric Antonow，Ashley Murphy 和 Sarah Caldwell 为这次对话建议主题和问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you enjoy this podcast, don't forget to subscribe and follow it on your favorite podcasting app or YouTube.
zh: 如果你喜欢这个播客，别忘了在你最喜欢的播客应用或 YouTube 上订阅并关注它。

speaker: Unknown
en: It helps tremendously.
zh: 这会有巨大的帮助。

speaker: Unknown
en: And if you become an annual subscriber of my newsletter, you get 19 incredible products for free for an entire year.
zh: 如果你成为我简报的年度订阅者，你将在整整一年内免费获得 19 个令人难以置信的产品。

speaker: Unknown
en: Including, Lovable, Replit, Bold, gamma, Innate and Linear, Devon, Posttalk, Superhuman descript, Whisper Flow, Perplexity.
zh: 包括 Lovable，Replit，Bold，gamma，Innate 和 Linear，Devon，Posttalk，Superhuman descript，Whisper Flow，Perplexity。

speaker: Unknown
en: Warp, Granola, Magic Patterns, Raycast, ChapiRD, Mobbit, and Stripe Atlas.
zh: Warp，Granola，Magic Patterns，Raycast，ChapiRD，Mobbit，以及 Stripe Atlas。

speaker: Unknown
en: Head on over to lennysnewsletter.com and click product pass.
zh: 前往 lennysnewsletter.com 并点击 product pass。

speaker: Unknown
en: With that, I bring you Molly Graham after a short word from our sponsors.
zh: 话虽如此，简短地感谢赞助商后，我为你带来 Molly Graham。

speaker: Unknown
en: Today's episode is brought to you by DX, the developer intelligence platform designed by leading researchers.
zh: 今天的节目由 DX 赞助，这是一个由领先研究人员设计的开发者智能平台。

speaker: Unknown
en: To thrive in the AI era, organizations need to adapt quickly.
zh: 要在 AI 时代蓬勃发展，组织需要快速适应。

speaker: Unknown
en: But many organization leaders struggle to answer pressing questions like, which tools are working?
zh: 但许多组织领导者难以回答紧迫的问题，比如哪些工具有效？

speaker: Unknown
en: How are they being used?
zh: 它们是如何被使用的？

speaker: Unknown
en: What's actually driving value?
zh: 什么真正在驱动价值？

speaker: Unknown
en: DX provides the data and insights that leaders need to navigate this shift.
zh: DX 提供领导者应对这种转变所需的数据和见解。

speaker: Unknown
en: With DX, companies like Dropbox, booking.com, Addien, and Intercom get a deep understanding of how AI is providing value to their developers.
zh: 有了 DX，像 Dropbox，booking.com，Addien 和 Intercom 这样的公司可以深入了解 AI 如何为其开发者提供价值。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what impact AI is having on engineering productivity.
zh: 以及 AI 对工程生产力产生了什么影响。

speaker: Unknown
en: To learn more, visit DX's website at getdx.com/lenny.
zh: 欲了解更多，请访问 getdx.com/lenny 的 DX 网站。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's getdx.com/lenny.
zh: 那就是 getdx.com/lenny。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you're a founder, the hardest part of starting a company isn't having the idea.
zh: 如果你是创始人，创业最难的部分不是有点子。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's scaling the business without getting buried in back office work.
zh: 而是在不被后台工作埋没的情况下扩展业务。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's where Brex comes in.
zh: 这就是 Brex 登场的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: Brex is the intelligent finance platform for founders.
zh: Brex 是创始人的智能财务平台。

speaker: Unknown
en: With Brex, you get high limit corporate cards, easy banking, high yield treasury, plus a team of AI agents that handle manual finance tasks for you.
zh: 有了 Brex，你会得到高额度企业卡、简易银行服务、高收益国库券，还有一个 AI 智能体团队为你处理手动财务任务。

speaker: Unknown
en: They'll do all the stuff that you don't want to do, like file your expenses, scour transactions for waste, and run reports all according to your rules.
zh: 它们会做你不想做的所有事情，比如归档你的开支、搜寻交易中的浪费，并根据你的规则运行报告。

speaker: Unknown
en: With Brex's AI agents, you can move faster while staying in full control.
zh: 有了 Brex 的 AI 智能体，你可以在保持完全控制的同时行动得更快。

speaker: Unknown
en: One in three startups in the United States already runs on Brex.
zh: 美国有三分之一的初创公司已经在 Brex 上运行了。

speaker: Unknown
en: You can too at brex.com.
zh: 你也可以在 brex.com 上做到。

speaker: Unknown
en: Molly, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
zh: Molly，非常感谢你来到这里，欢迎来到播客。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thanks, Lenny.
zh: 谢谢，Lenny。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm excited to be here.
zh: 我很高兴来到这里。

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like this conversation was in an inevitability.
zh: 我感觉这场对话是不可避免的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like you're the kind of guest where it's like, we will do this someday.
zh: 我觉得你是那种就像，我们终有一天会做这事的嘉宾。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm such a fan of your stuff.
zh: 我是你所有作品的一个粉丝。

speaker: Unknown
en: I've read all the stuff you've put out there over the years.
zh: 我读了你这些年发布的所有东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're going to be talking about the best frameworks and mindsets that you've developed over the years that have been really helpful to you, to founders, to companies that you've worked with to help them with growth and scale and change and all the stuff that comes with success.
zh: 我们将讨论你多年来开发的最佳框架和思维模式，这些对你、对你合作过的创始人、对公司真的很有帮助，帮助他们处理增长、规模、变化以及伴随成功而来的所有事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: The way I think about this, I want to make this the greatest hits of Molly Graham.
zh: 关于这个，我的想法是，我想把这做成 Molly Graham 的精选集。

speaker: Unknown
en: Love it.
zh: 爱死这个说法了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I sourced what I think are the greatest hits from a lot of colleagues that you've worked with, a lot of people you've worked with.
zh: 所以我从你合作的很多同事那里收集了我认为是精选集的东西，从很多和你共事过的人那里。

speaker: Unknown
en: We've chatted about the stuff that you find other people find most helpful.
zh: 我们聊了那些你觉得其他人觉得最有用的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: So we're going to be going through all that stuff.
zh: 所以我们将要过一遍所有那些东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: But let's help people understand why they should listen to this advice.
zh: 但让我们帮大家理解为什么他们应该听这些建议。

speaker: Unknown
en: What's kind of the backstory on these frameworks?
zh: 这些框架的背景故事是怎样的？

speaker: Unknown
en: Where did they come from?
zh: 它们来自哪里？

speaker: Unknown
en: Where did you develop them?
zh: 你是在哪里开发它们的？

speaker: Unknown
en: Tell us that story.
zh: 告诉我们那个故事。

speaker: Unknown
en: So first of all, Ami Vora, who you have had on your podcast, once said to me that all advice is just someone telling you what they did.
zh: 所以首先，Ami Vora，也就是你播客上的那位嘉宾，有一次对我说，所有建议都只是某人在告诉你他们做了什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I always think about that.
zh: 而我一直都在想这件事。

speaker: Unknown
en: Because I really think that basically what I tell people is I've made every single mistake in the book.
zh: 因为我真的认为基本上我告诉人们的是，我犯下了书里所有的错误。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then I got to the end of the book and I started inventing new mistakes.
zh: 然后我翻到了书的末尾，我开始发明新的错误。

speaker: Unknown
en: So mostly what I feel is that I like sharing my stories because I want to help people.
zh: 所以大部分我的感受是，我喜欢分享我的故事，因为我想帮助人们。

speaker: Unknown
en: I want to help people not make the same mistakes I did.
zh: 我想帮助人们不犯我犯过的同样的错误。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I also want to help people make sense of what they're experiencing.
zh: 而且我也想帮助人们理解他们正在经历的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I started in tech in 2007.
zh: 但我是在 2007 年进入科技行业的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I actually started at Google the week the iPhone launched and a lot of my scaling battle scars come from a couple of experiences.
zh: 我实际上是在 iPhone 发布的那一周加入的 Google，而我很多关于扩展的伤痕来自几段经历。

speaker: Unknown
en: They come from a year and a half at Google, which is not very long.
zh: 它们来自在 Google 的一年半，这并不长。

speaker: Unknown
en: And Google was pretty big when I was there.
zh: 当我在那里的时候，Google 已经很大了。

speaker: Unknown
en: It has thousands of employees.
zh: 它有数千名员工。

speaker: Unknown
en: But my department, which was the communications department, was 25 people when I joined and it grew in nine months to 125 people.
zh: 但我的部门，也就是通讯部门，我加入时是 25 人，在九个月内增长到了 125 人。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that was really my first experience with just all the sort of things that I still talk about today.
zh: 那真的是我第一次体验那些直到今天我仍在谈论的所有事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: In terms of what it feels like to grow really, really fast and sort of all the tools that I started developing from there.
zh: 关于增长真的非常快是什么感觉，以及我从那里开始开发的所有工具。

speaker: Unknown
en: After Google, I left and followed Cheryl Sandberg and Elliot Schrage to Facebook.
zh: 在 Google 之后，我离开并跟随 Cheryl Sandberg 和 Elliot Schrage 去了 Facebook。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I spent five years at Facebook.
zh: 然后我在 Facebook 待了五年。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I joined Facebook in 2008, and it's important context because it was 80 million users at the time.
zh: 我在 2008 年加入 Facebook，这背景很重要，因为当时有 8000 万用户。

speaker: Unknown
en: We were smaller than MySpace.
zh: 我们比 MySpace 还小。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was 270 million in revenue, 500 employees.
zh: 它是 2.7 亿美元的收入，500 名员工。

speaker: Unknown
en: It did not feel inevitable.
zh: 它感觉并不是不可避免的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Most people thought we were going to sell it to Microsoft.
zh: 大多数人以为我们会把它卖给 Microsoft。

speaker: Unknown
en: When I told people I was going there, they were like, isn't that place just like a site for college kids?
zh: 当我告诉人们我要去那里时，他们会说，那不就是大学生用的网站吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I was there for five years and it was a crazy five years.
zh: 所以我在那里待了五年，那是疯狂的五年。

speaker: Unknown
en: When I left, it was 5,500 employees, five billion in revenue, over a billion users.
zh: 当我离开时，它是 5500 名员工，50 亿美元的收入，超过 10 亿用户。

speaker: Unknown
en: So a huge amount of what I experienced, what I write about, what I talk about in Glue Club, which is the community that I run, comes from that rapid scale at Google and Facebook.
zh: 所以我经历的大部分内容，我写的内容，我在 Glue Club 里谈论的内容，Glue Club 是我运营的一个社区，都源于在 Google 和 Facebook 的那段时间的快速扩张。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I also, I left Facebook right after we went public, about six months after we went public.
zh: 但我还在，我在我们上市后不久就离开了 Facebook，大约在我们上市六个月后。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I only like doing jobs that I'm highly unqualified for.
zh: 而且我只喜欢做那些我远不合格的工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: I like being on learning curves so steep that I'm scared I'm going to fall off.
zh: 我喜欢待在如此陡峭的学习曲线上，以至于我很害怕会掉下来。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I left and I wanted to learn what it took to build something from nothing.
zh: 所以我离开了，我想知道白手起家需要具备什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I joined this little startup founded by Brett Taylor, a startup called Quip.
zh: 于是我加入了这个由 Brett Taylor 创办的小型初创公司，一家叫 Quip 的公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: I joined a couple of months before we launched and ran everything that wasn't product and engineering there for him.
zh: 我在我们上线前几个月加入，负责管理除了产品和工程以外的所有事情，为他负责。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that was such a valuable experience to me because the experience of building something from nothing is actually quite different than the experience of holding on for dear life while things are scaling so fast around you.
zh: 这对我来说是一次非常有价值的经历，因为白手起家的经历实际上与周围事物发展如此之快时拼命维持生命的经历截然不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it really taught me about all the tools and skills you need to go from zero to one and then from one to two and how lonely it can be to build something.
zh: 它真的教会了我从零到一，再从一到二所需的所有工具和技能，以及建造东西是多么孤独。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we eventually sold that company to Salesforce.
zh: 我们最终把那家公司卖给了 Salesforce。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then again, only take jobs I'm highly unqualified for.
zh: 然后再次强调，我只做那些我远不合格的工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: But the last really chaotic scaling experience I had was actually helping Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan start their philanthropy, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.
zh: 但我最后一次真正的混乱扩张经历，实际上是帮助 Mark Zuckerberg 和 Priscilla Chan 启动他们的慈善事业，也就是 Chan Zuckerberg Initiative。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I basically helped them for the first two years of its existence or its sort of like first full existence.
zh: 我基本上在它存在的前两年，或者说是它最初完整存在的两年里帮助了他们。

speaker: Unknown
en: And philanthropy sounds calm.
zh: 慈善事业听起来很平静。

speaker: Unknown
en: You know what I mean?
zh: 你懂我的意思吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: We're like, oh, giving money away.
zh: 我们就像，噢，送钱嘛。

speaker: Unknown
en: Must be so peaceful over there.
zh: 那里肯定很平静。

speaker: Unknown
en: And CZI grew from, I think the week I joined, it was 30 people and we bought two companies that week and it grew to 250 people that year.
zh: 而 CZI 从，我想我加入的那一周，是 30 人，那一周我们收购了两家公司，那一年它增长到了 250 人。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it was like using every single tool in my toolkit that I had taken from every other job that I'd had.
zh: 这就像用我工具箱里的每一个工具，那些我从我以前做过的工作中拿来的工具。

speaker: Unknown
en: So my advice and frameworks, like I said, come from having made a lot of mistakes.
zh: 所以我的建议和框架，就像我说的，来自于犯过很多错误。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I've also sort of made a personal study over the last 18 years, believe it or not.
zh: 但我也在过去 18 年里，信不信由你，某种程度上做了一项个人的研究。

speaker: Unknown
en: Essentially what does it take to thrive inside growing and changing companies, not just to hang on for dear life.
zh: 本质上是在发展变化的公司里茁壮成长需要什么，而不仅仅是拼命维持生命。

speaker: Unknown
en: What does it take to lead in the face of constant change?
zh: 在持续变化面前进行领导需要什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: And really the other piece that I find truly fascinating is what genuinely makes the difference between a business that grows but then plateaus versus these generational businesses.
zh: 而我真正觉得非常迷人的另一点是，到底是什么让那些增长但随后进入平台期的业务与这些代际企业之间产生了差异。

speaker: Unknown
en: The ones that go on forever.
zh: 那些永续经营的公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: Sort of the difference between a Twitter or MySpace and a Facebook.
zh: 有点像 Twitter 或 MySpace 与 Facebook 之间的区别。

speaker: Unknown
en: Billions in revenue versus hundreds of billions in revenue.
zh: 数十亿美元的收入与数千亿美元的收入之间的区别。

speaker: Unknown
en: So what I like to do is take my experience and use it to help other leaders.
zh: 所以我喜欢做的是利用我的经验来帮助其他领导者。

speaker: Unknown
en: I want to give people tools that work.
zh: 我想给人们提供行之有效的工具。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I also want to be honest about how hard all of this stuff really is.
zh: 我也想诚实地说明这一切到底有多难。

zh: 那才是真正重要的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: Everything else is just Bob.
zh: 其他一切都只是 Bob。

speaker: Unknown
en: Is there a rule of thumb for when it actually, when you shouldn't give away your Legos?
zh: 关于何时真正，何时不该交出你的乐高，有什么经验法则吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: When it's like, okay, maybe you should fight back on this layering or whatever.
zh: 比如，好吧，也许你应该对这种 layered 或其他情况进行反击。

speaker: Unknown
en: No rule of thumb.
zh: 没有经验法则。

speaker: Unknown
en: In general, I would actually say embracing change is far better than fighting it.
zh: 总的来说，我其实会说拥抱改变比与之对抗要好得多。

speaker: Unknown
en: And almost invariably, you cannot see what is around the corner, but it is almost always the thing to focus on.
zh: 而且几乎无一例外，你看不到拐角处是什么，但它几乎总是值得关注的重点。

speaker: Unknown
en: A lot of times I think inside of change, we get focused on the past, and one of the most valuable things you can do as a manager and a leader is help people focus on the future.
zh: 很多时候我认为在面对改变时，我们会关注过去，而作为管理者和领导者你能做的最有价值的事情之一就是帮助人们关注未来。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think... I'm sure there are times when people have done it and regretted it and it has led them somewhere.
zh: 我认为……我确信有些时候人们这么做了并且后悔了，这把他们带到了某个地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think being layered, for example, is one of the hardest things for people inside these experiences where someone brings in a manager above you.
zh: 我认为被 layered，例如，是这些经历中人们最难面对的事情之一，比如有人招了一个经理在你上面。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I've also seen so many stories of that ending up being a great thing for someone.
zh: 但我也看过很多故事，那最终对某人来说是一件很好的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: Even though they couldn't see it at the time.
zh: 尽管他们当时看不到这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: So in general, I would just say, step into the future and let the past go and see what you're going to learn.
zh: 所以总的来说，我只会说，迈向未来，放下过去，看看你会学到什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: And sometimes you'll learn that it's time to leave or that this isn't the right pile of Legos for you.
zh: 有时你会学到是时候离开了，或者这堆乐高并不适合你。

speaker: Unknown
en: But it'll end up taking you somewhere that's worth exploring.
zh: 但它最终会把你带到一个值得探索的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: Holding onto things almost always leads us to the worst version of ourselves.
zh: 紧抓不放几乎总是会导致我们变成最糟糕的自己。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's a very Buddhist way of thinking too.
zh: 这也是一种非常佛教的思维方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: Just don't cling.
zh: 就是不要执着。

speaker: Molly Graham
en: There you go.
zh: 就是那样。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think another part of this metaphor, I don't know if you think of it this way.
zh: 我认为这个隐喻的另一个部分，我不知道你是不是这么想的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Is the Legos aren't even your Legos, right?
zh: 是那些乐高甚至不是你的乐高，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: They're like the CEO's Legos, the shareholders' Legos.
zh: 它们是 CEO 的乐高，是股东的乐高。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you think they're your Legos, but no, you're not in charge.
zh: 所以你认为它们是你的乐高，但不，你并不负责。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, it is... I will say one of the hard-earned things is it can feel very emotional and it can feel very personal.
zh: 嗯，它是……我要说这是辛苦得来的一课，它可能感觉非常情绪化，也可能感觉非常个人化。

speaker: Unknown
en: It can feel like your work... I don't know, it can feel like your life is on the line sometimes.
zh: 它可能感觉你的工作……我不知道，它可能有时感觉你的生活命悬一线。

speaker: Unknown
en: Just your work life.
zh: 只是你的工作生活。

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh, gosh, this matters so much.
zh: 天哪，这太重要了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And one of the things that you learn as you get more senior and just have seen stuff is it's going to be okay.
zh: 而随着你变得资深，见多识广，你会学到的一件事就是，一切都会好起来的。

speaker: Unknown
en: A friend of mine says, careers are long and nobody tells you that.
zh: 我的一个朋友说，职业生涯很漫长，没人告诉你这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: But they're long.
zh: 但它们确实很漫长。

speaker: Unknown
en: And this moment feels so dire and it feels so hard and it feels scary and it's going to be okay.
zh: 而这一刻感觉如此危急，感觉如此艰难，感觉如此可怕，而且一切都会好起来的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So yeah, it is hard to know in the moment.
zh: 所以是的，很难在当下知道这些。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think the story is going to be long and this is going to be one chapter or maybe even a part of a chapter, not a whole chapter.
zh: 我认为这个故事会很长，而这只是其中一章，或者甚至是一章的一部分，而不是完整的一章。

speaker: Unknown
en: So embrace the length.
zh: 所以拥抱长度。

speaker: Unknown
en: To build on that point, I've realized this is my fourth career doing what I do now.
zh: 为了以此为基础，我意识到这是我职业生涯中第四次做我现在做的事。

speaker: Unknown
en: Whatever the hell this is.
zh: 不管这到底是个什么东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: I was a engineer and then I was a founder.
zh: 我曾是个工程师，然后我是个创始人。

speaker: Unknown
en: Then I was a product manager, and then what the hell I do now.
zh: 然后我是个产品经理，然后就是我到底在做的这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: Whatever this is, that's a whole different path.
zh: 不管这是什么，那完全是另一条路。

speaker: Unknown
en: You don't have a name for it yet, Lenny?
zh: Lenny，你还没给它起个名字吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't.
zh: 我没有。

speaker: Unknown
en: I hate all the terms people use for this world.
zh: 我讨厌人们用来指代这个领域的所有术语。

speaker: Unknown
en: Somebody called me an influencer and I almost ripped their face off.
zh: 有人叫我是网红（influencer），我差点把他们的脸给撕了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: [inaudible 00:23:02].

speaker: Unknown
en: [inaudible 00:23:02].

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, man.
zh: 是的，伙计。

speaker: Unknown
en: The most interesting careers are winding and they have starts and stops and failures and successes and control.
zh: 最有趣的职业生涯是蜿蜒曲折的，它们有起有停，有失败有成功，还有掌控。

speaker: Unknown
en: Anybody that's been through a lot of this stuff, control is usually not the name of the game.
zh: 任何经历过很多这类事情的人，掌控通常不是游戏的名称。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's usually just like, "Let's see what happens.
zh: 通常就像是，“让我们看看会发生什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're going to try this and we're going to see what happens next."
zh: 我们要试试这个，然后我们要看看接下来会发生什么。”

speaker: Unknown
en: This is a great segue to another framework that I've heard from folks you've worked with that have been really impactful on them.
zh: 这是一个很好的过渡，转到另一个框架，我从你合作过的人那里听到的，对他们产生了真正的影响。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, Sarah Caldwell, who's a big deal at OpenAI, she told me that the framework that helped her most in her career is something that you call the J-Curve versus Stairs career growth framework.
zh: 所以，Sarah Caldwell，她是 OpenAI 的大人物，她告诉我，在她职业生涯中帮助最大的框架是你所谓的 J 曲线对比阶梯式职业成长框架。

speaker: Unknown
en: Talk about what that's about.
zh: 谈谈那是关于什么的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I actually gave a TED Talk about this one a couple of years ago because I am so passionate about it, but you can listen to the very packaged eight-minute version of this, but I will tell you the real story because it's very relevant to a lot of folks that listen to your podcast.
zh: 几年前我实际上做了一个关于这个的 TED 演讲，因为我对此非常充满热情，但你可以听那个非常包装好的八分钟版本，但我会告诉你真实的故事，因为它与很多听你播客的人非常相关。

speaker: Unknown
en: I was at Facebook for five years.
zh: 我在 Facebook 待了五年。

speaker: Unknown
en: Like I said, the first two years I was in HR and I was doing employment branding and culture work and I was ready to stay there.
zh: 就像我说的，前两年我在人力资源部，我在做雇主品牌和文化工作，我准备好待在那里。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think I had in my head I was going to stay there until we went public, that was my plan just because I wanted to help the company through that moment, again, in my head.
zh: 我想我在脑子里我打算待在那里直到我们上市，那是我的计划，只是因为我想帮助公司度过那个时刻，再次强调，是在我的脑子里。

speaker: Unknown
en: This guy that many people know, Chamath Palihapitiya, came to me and Chamath ran growth and mobile at the time.
zh: 很多人都知道的这个人，Chamath Palihapitiya，来找我，Chamath 当时负责增长和移动端。

speaker: Unknown
en: And he came to me and we had lunch and he said in his very Chamath way, "You're useless.
zh: 他来找我，我们一起吃了午餐，他说着非常 Chamath 风格的话，“你真没用。

speaker: Unknown
en: What are you doing in HR?
zh: 你在人力资源部干什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: This is stupid.
zh: 这太蠢了。

speaker: Unknown
en: You should come work for me."
zh: 你应该来为我工作。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And anybody that knows Chamath is like, "Yes, that is actually what he said."
zh: 任何认识 Chamath 的人都会说，“是的，那实际上就是他说的话。”

speaker: Unknown
en: He managed to insult you and compliment you in one sentence.
zh: 他设法在一句话里侮辱了你又夸奖了你。

speaker: Unknown
en: He gave me all these options on his team.
zh: 他给了我他在团队里的所有这些选项。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then the last one he said to me was like, "I'm going to go build a mobile phone.
zh: 然后他对我说的最后一个选项是，“我要去造一部手机。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you want to come do that with me?"
zh: 你想跟我一起做那个吗？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And I had four simultaneous reactions.
zh: 我有四个同时的反应。

speaker: Unknown
en: The first was like, " That is incredibly stupid.
zh: 第一个是，“那真是蠢得难以置信。

speaker: Unknown
en: Why are we doing that?"
zh: 我们为什么要那样做？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And then it was like, "Is that actually a thing that we're doing?"
zh: 然后是，“这实际上是我们正在做的一件事吗？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And then it was like, "Whoa, I think that sounds kind of fun."
zh: 然后是，“哇，我觉得那听起来有点好玩。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I left the conversation at Chamath and I went and asked my boss, Lori Goler, who's the head of people at Facebook for a very long time, like, "Is this actually something we're doing?"
zh: 所以我结束了和 Chamath 的谈话，然后我去问我的老板，Lori Goler，她是 Facebook 的人力资源负责人很长时间，我问，“这实际上是我们正在做的一件事吗？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And she was like, "I can't believe he offered you that, whatever."
zh: 她说，“我不敢相信他给了你那个提议，不管了。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And I basically just could not get it out of my head, but it didn't make any sense, A, that Chamath had asked me because I was in HR.
zh: 我基本上就是无法把它从我的脑海里赶出去，但这毫无道理，A，Chamath 问我是因为我在人力资源部。

speaker: Unknown
en: Like, "What am I doing?
zh: 就像，“我在做什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't absolutely jack shit about mobile."
zh: 我对移动端一窍不通。”

speaker: Unknown
en: But I had worked on a project with him and I guess he thought I was smart.
zh: 但我和他一起做一个项目，我想他觉得我很聪明。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I talked to Cheryl and she was like, "Well, that project will be dead in two months, but you can do it because you'll still have a job here."
zh: 我和 Cheryl 谈过，她说，“嗯，那个项目会在两个月内死掉，但你可以做，因为你还会有工作在这里。”

speaker: Unknown
en: My dad was like, "Well, don't do that. "
zh: 我爸说，“嗯，别做那个。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And anyway, a lot of very wise people being like, "Don't do that."
zh: 不管怎么说，很多非常明智的人都在说，“别做那个。”

speaker: Unknown
en: But I kind of couldn't get out of my head.
zh: 但我有点无法摆脱这种想法。

speaker: Unknown
en: And my friend said to me, "You've proven you're really good at this sort of company-wide project management and HR.
zh: 我朋友对我说，你已经证明了你非常擅长这种全公司范围的项目管理和人力资源工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: Why don't you go show yourself how actually good you are?
zh: 你为什么不去向你自己展示你实际上有多好呢？

speaker: Unknown
en: Is this transferable?"
zh: 这是可迁移的吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: So, I took the job and I spent the next six months feeling like an absolute idiot.
zh: 所以，我接受了这份工作，在接下来的六个月里，我觉得自己简直像个白痴。

speaker: Unknown
en: I basically felt like a total jackass all the time.
zh: 我基本上一直觉得自己完全像个傻瓜。

speaker: Unknown
en: I was sitting in rooms with these brilliant people asking the dumbest questions of my life and at the end of the six months, Chamath, I think, took a lot of pride in giving me the lowest performance rating I've ever gotten in my life, and it just felt like falling off a cliff.
zh: 我和那些聪明人坐在房间里，问着我这辈子问过的最愚蠢的问题，而在六个月结束时，Chamath，我想，非常自豪地给了我有生以来最低的绩效评分，那感觉就像从悬崖上掉下来一样。

speaker: Unknown
en: Then, slowly, I remember I had been doing all these trips to Taiwan because we were actually working on hardware and I, at some point, came back from Taiwan and I drew on a whiteboard for him the layout of a mobile phone and trying to explain to him why something he wanted to do was not possible.
zh: 后来，慢慢地，我记得我一直在去台湾旅行，因为我们实际上是在做硬件，我在某个时候从台湾回来，我在白板上为他画了一个手机的布局，试图向他解释为什么他想要做的事情是不可能的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I so vividly remember walking out of that meeting being like, "Oh, I actually know things."
zh: 我如此清晰地记得走出那个会议室时的情景，心想，哦，我确实懂这些东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And slowly then, over the following three years, I became an expert in mobile.
zh: 然后在接下来的三年里，我慢慢地成为了移动领域的专家。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I basically... The phone itself was a giant failure, massive, costly failure for Facebook, but it was not a failure for me.
zh: 我基本上……这款手机本身是一个巨大的失败，对 Facebook 来说是代价惨重的巨大失败，但这对我来说并不是失败。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was a huge job that taught me that I was capable of things that I never could have dreamed of if I had stayed in HR.
zh: 这是一份巨大的工作，它教会了我，我有能力做那些如果我一直留在人力资源部永远无法梦想的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: It set me up to be capable of taking on things that I didn't know about.
zh: 它让我有能力去承担那些我不了解的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: Chamath, when he pitched me on this job, actually drew me a picture on a whiteboard.
zh: Chamath，当他向我推销这份工作时，实际上在白板上给我画了一张图。

speaker: Unknown
en: He said, "Look, you can stay..." The way a lot of people do careers is a set of stairs.
zh: 他说，你看，你可以留……很多人做职业规划的方式就像是一组楼梯。

speaker: Unknown
en: "You can be boring."
zh: 你可以很无聊。

speaker: Unknown
en: To use Chamath, "And stay on these stairs.
zh: 用 Chamath 的话说，而且留在这组楼梯上。

speaker: Unknown
en: Just walk up the stairs and you'll get promoted every two years and your title will change from manager to senior manager to director to senior director, whatever."
zh: 只要走上楼梯，你每两年就会得到晋升，你的头衔会从经理变成高级经理，再到总监、高级总监等等。

speaker: Unknown
en: And he was like, "But that is boring."
zh: 然后他说，但这很无聊。

speaker: Unknown
en: And he's like, "The much more fun careers are like jumping off cliffs."
zh: 他说，更有趣的职业道路就像跳下悬崖。

speaker: Unknown
en: Basically, that you jump off this thing and you do fall for a period of time.
zh: 基本上，就是你要跳下这个东西，而且你确实会坠落一段时间。

speaker: Unknown
en: I always like to say it's about six to nine months, but then this thing happens where you climb out.
zh: 我总是喜欢说这大约是六到九个月，但随后会发生一些事情，让你爬出来。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the picture he drew had this J-curve sort of basically leading you to places that are way beyond where the stairs could ever get you.
zh: 他画的图上有一条 J 曲线，基本上把你带到楼梯永远无法到达的遥远的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: And to be totally honest, that has been my experience.
zh: 坦率地说，那就是我的经历。

speaker: Unknown
en: That taking risks, accepting the sort of terrible fall and that experience of falling has been more than worth it.
zh: 冒险，接受那种可怕的坠落以及那种坠落的感觉，是非常值得的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Part of the reason why Sarah mentions it is that I do give this sort of talk to people that are inside of really fast-growing companies, because it's such an important place to let go of Legos and jump off cliffs because there's so much opportunity.
zh: Sarah 提到它的部分原因是，我确实会给那些在真正快速增长的公司里的人做这种类型的演讲，因为这是一个放下积木并跳下悬崖的重要地方，因为有太多的机会。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it is a place where if you prove to people that you're actually good, if they believe that you are the kind of person that they can use to do lots of things, you can get these opportunities that you are just so deeply unqualified for, but they can take you to places that you could never have imagined.
zh: 在这个地方，如果你向人们证明你实际上很棒，如果他们相信你是那种可以被用来做很多事情的人，你就能得到那些你完全不够格的机会，但它们能把你带到你无法想象的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: You can come out of those companies with skills that no one would ever have reasonably hired you to do.
zh: 你可以带着那些没有人会合理雇佣你去做的技能离开这些公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I ended my time at Facebook in product and did business development and hardware and a whole bunch of the stuff along the way.
zh: 但我在 Facebook 的最后一段时光是在产品部门，并且做了业务开发和硬件以及一路上的一堆东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And again, nobody would've hired me to do that at the beginning, but it's just because I kept saying yes to things.
zh: 同样，起初没有人会雇佣我做那些，但这只是因为我对所有事情都一直说是。

speaker: Unknown
en: Molly, I got tingles listening to this story.
zh: Molly，听着这个故事我浑身起了鸡皮疙瘩。

speaker: Unknown
en: Wow.
zh: 哇。

speaker: Unknown
en: Does it sound familiar, Lenny?
zh: 这听起来很熟悉吗，Lenny？

speaker: Unknown
en: It does.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I want to ask, jumping off a cliff, sometimes you fall, really fall and you keep falling.
zh: 我想问一下，跳下悬崖，有时候你会坠落，真的坠落，并且一直坠落。

speaker: Unknown
en: Are there any kind of traits of like, "Okay, this is one that might be a J-Curve and worth the risk of falling, and this is when you should probably just not, let's not do this".
zh: 有没有什么特征可以判断，好吧，这是一个可能属于 J 曲线并且值得冒坠落风险的，而这个是时候可能就不应该，让我们不要做这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I just think there are different kinds of fear.
zh: 我只是认为有不同种类的恐惧。

speaker: Unknown
en: We talk a lot about this in Glue Club because one of the thing, there is a financial fear, right?
zh: 我们在 Glue Club 里经常谈论这个，因为其中一件事是，有一种对财务的恐惧，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: Leaving a job and taking a job that has financial risk associated with it, or leaving a job and taking time off, which is something that I spend a lot of time talking to people about, you got to do the math and you got to... Sometimes there is a type of fear that is telling you like, "This is not the right time."
zh: 辞职并接受一份有财务风险的工作，或者辞职并休假，这是我花很多时间和人们谈论的事情，你得算算账，你得……有时候有一种恐惧在告诉你，现在不是时候。

speaker: Unknown
en: Or, "I don't want to be financially anxious for months and months and months."
zh: 或者，我不想在好几个月好几个月里对财务感到焦虑。

speaker: Unknown
en: I use finances because it's the most concrete example of a type of fear that you should actually listen to.

en: Essentially, that is going to be harder or easier based on whatever the shape of the ocean is, right?
zh: 本质上，这取决于海洋的形状，会变得更难或更容易，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: If it's really choppy, it's harder, if it's smooth and calm, it's going to be easy to get to your goals.
zh: 如果波涛汹涌，就会更难；如果风平浪静，到达目标就会很容易。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, the Waterline basically asks the question like, "What is going on under the water?
zh: 所以，吃水线基本上提出了一个问题，“水面之下发生了什么？”

speaker: Unknown
en: What is going on that's making it harder or easier to get to your goals?"
zh: 发生了什么让到达目标变得更难或更容易？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And there's essentially four things underneath the water and they are in a descending order.
zh: 水面之下基本上有四样东西，它们是按降序排列的。

speaker: Unknown
en: The surface level is what's called structural things.
zh: 表面层叫做结构性事务。

speaker: Unknown
en: Basically, structural things are like goal setting, vision, roles, expectations, kind of the structures you put in place to make a team and a company and a business make sense, that touch every single member of the team.
zh: 基本上，结构性事务就像目标设定、愿景、角色、期望，也就是为了让团队、公司和业务讲得通而建立的结构，这涉及团队的每一位成员。

speaker: Unknown
en: Right below that is something called dynamics, which is essentially how the team works together.
zh: 就在那之下的是叫做团队动力（dynamics），本质上是团队如何协作。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's culture, it's decision making, it's how we resolve conflict, all the sort of like interwoven pieces of how teams work together.
zh: 它是文化、决策制定、我们如何解决冲突，所有这些交织在一起的团队协作方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then below that is interpersonal, so basically relationships between two people and all the things that come with us being humans.
zh: 再下面是人际层面，也就是两个人之间的关系，以及我们要作为人类所带来的所有事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then the bottom is intrapersonal, meaning within one person, challenges and issues there.
zh: 最底层是个人内心（intrapersonal），意味着在一个人的内部，那里的挑战和问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: The interesting thing about this model is that most people, when something's going wrong on a team, a lot of times we always go to the bottom.
zh: 这个模型的有趣之处在于，大多数人，当团队出现问题的时候，很多时候我们总是直接去到底层。

speaker: Unknown
en: We go to the people.
zh: 我们去找人。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're like, "The people aren't getting along, that person's having a rough moment."
zh: 我们会说，“这些人相处不来，那个人遇到了困难。”

speaker: Unknown
en: We go to the humans, but the rule with the Waterline Model, which is very memorable, is you snorkel before you scuba.
zh: 我们去找人，但是吃水线模型的规则非常难忘，那就是在深潜之前先浮潜。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, 80% of problems on teams actually happen because of structural issues or dynamics issues.
zh: 所以，团队上 80% 的问题实际上是因为结构性问题或动力问题而发生的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, when there are problems on your team, where you start is at the top, you start structural issues.
zh: 所以，当你的团队出现问题时，你从顶部开始，从结构性问题开始。

speaker: Unknown
en: And one of my biggest things that I say all the time over and over again inside of Glue Club is, "Your only goal as a manager, if you do nothing else, is clear roles and clear expectations.
zh: 我在 Glue Club 内部一遍又一遍说的最重要的一件事是，“作为管理者，如果你不做其他事情，你唯一的目标就是明确的角色和明确的期望。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's it."
zh: 就是这样。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Because honestly, I've taken over a lot of teams in my life and almost always I show up and it turns out that no one knows what their job is and no one knows what success looks like.
zh: 因为老实说，我在生活中接管过很多团队，几乎总是我一到就发现，没有人知道他们的工作是什么，也没有人知道成功是什么样子的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And if you can make those two things clear, which again is at the snorkel level, it will fix a huge percentage of other issues on a team.
zh: 如果你能把这两件事弄清楚，这又是在浮潜层面，它将修复团队中很大一部分的其他问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: But the main thing is where you start and just always sort of starting at that structural level or the dynamics level and not sort of immediately going to the people and all that.
zh: 但主要关键在于你从哪里开始，总是从那个结构层面或动力层面开始，而不是直接去找人，不要做那些事。

speaker: Unknown
en: Because yes, people cause all sorts of problems, but a lot of times the problems are happening because they're existing inside of a structure that's confusing.
zh: 因为是的，人会导致各种问题，但很多时候问题发生是因为他们处在一个令人困惑的结构中。

speaker: Unknown
en: Another very vivid metaphor and just, I love how it builds on it with the snorkeling.
zh: 另一个非常生动的隐喻，我只是很喜欢它是如何建立在浮潜之上的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Okay.
zh: 好的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, just to be super clear about this, the takeaway here is, you have a problem with your team, with the company, many people think it's, they jump to the people are the problem.
zh: 所以，为了把这一点说得超级清楚，这里的要点是，你的团队或公司有问题，很多人认为问题是人，他们跳到人就是问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: "They're not good enough, they're not working hard enough."
zh: “他们不够好，他们工作不够努力。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Really, what you're saying is, most often, the issue is not the person, it's the situation, whether it's the structure of how they're set up to work or the dynamics amongst the people.
zh: 真正的，你所说的是，大多数情况下，问题不是人，是处境，无论是他们被安排工作的结构还是人们之间的动力。

speaker: Unknown
en: And specifically what you're saying is that the role maybe isn't clear or what success means for that role is not clear.
zh: 具体所说的，角色可能不明确，或者该角色的成功意味着什么不明确。

speaker: Unknown
en: Every company I've worked with or advise, I often start with like, "What are the goals?"
zh: 我合作的或咨询的每一家公司，我经常从“目标是什么？”开始。

speaker: Unknown
en: And usually what you get the hack is, "Uh, not clear."
zh: 通常你得到的答案是，“呃，不清楚。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And that in and of itself is a structural issue, right?
zh: 这本身就是一个结构性问题，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: How can someone show up and decide what they're going to do with their day all day if the goals aren't clear, if they don't actually know what the priorities are?
zh: 如果目标不明确，如果他们实际上不知道优先级是什么，一个人怎么能到场并决定他们整天要做什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: And then it goes to, okay, role, right?
zh: 然后这就到了，好吧，角色，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: "Do I know what my job is?
zh: “我知道我的工作是什么吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Do I know what number I was hired to own and drive?"
zh: 我知道我被雇佣来负责和推动的数字是什么吗？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And then, "Do I know what success looks like?
zh: 然后，“我知道成功是什么样的吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: How does my role tie to that overall goal that the company has?"
zh: 我的角色如何与公司拥有的那个总体目标联系起来？”

speaker: Unknown
en: Just literally right there.
zh: 就真的在那里。

speaker: Unknown
en: You got probably 80% of problems inside of companies because this is the hard work of company building.
zh: 你可能遇到了公司内部 80% 的问题，因为这是公司建设的艰苦工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's the stuff that's not intuitive.
zh: 这是那些不直观的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: "How do you organize a group of people to know which direction to row?"
zh: “如何组织一群人知道朝哪个方向划船？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And that equation, again, I would say 80% of problems that I see, performance issues.
zh: 那个等式，同样，我会说我看到的 80% 的问题，绩效问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: I always start with, "Does this person actually know what you expect of them?"
zh: 我总是从，“这个人实际上知道你对他们的期望是什么吗？”开始。

speaker: Unknown
en: If not, go back to step one.
zh: 如果不知道，回到第一步。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know what I mean?
zh: 你明白我的意思吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Clarify expectations, so the Waterline Model is just helpful for reminding us, like, "Start at the top."
zh: 澄清期望，所以吃水线模型只是有助于提醒我们，比如，“从顶部开始。”

speaker: Unknown
en: So what would you do there?
zh: 那么你在那里会怎么做？

speaker: Unknown
en: Say you're a manager, you're having an issue with a team member, would you go and ask, "Hey, let's just make sure we're aligned on goals and roles."
zh: 假设你是一名经理，你与一名团队成员有问题，你会去问，“嘿，让我们确保我们在目标和角色上是一致的。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Is that how'd you approach it or is there a different approach?
zh: 那是你接近它的方式还是有不同的方法？

speaker: Unknown
en: So a lot of times what I do is two-sided, right?
zh: 所以很多时候我做的是双向的，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: So it's like, "Hey, here's what I'm seeing and tell me what's going on for you.
zh: 就像是，“嘿，这是我看到的，告诉我你那里发生了什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know X, Y, Z?"
zh: 你知道 X, Y, Z 吗？”

speaker: Unknown
en: When I take over a team, when I'm doing my listening tour, part of what I'm asking is, "What do you think your job is?
zh: 当我接手一个团队，当我进行我的聆听之旅时，我询问的一部分内容是，“你认为你的工作是什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: What number were you hired to drive?"
zh: 你被雇佣来推动的数字是多少？”

speaker: Unknown
en: Because what you'll find is often their picture is different than your picture.
zh: 因为你会发现，通常他们的图景与你的图景不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: You think you've been clear, you described an elephant and they spat out a tiger and that coming back to like, "Okay, no, we're building an elephant.
zh: 你以为你已经清楚了，你描述了一头大象，他们却吐出一只老虎，这就回到了，“好的，不，我们在建造一头大象。

speaker: Unknown
en: You're in charge of the trunk."
zh: 你负责象鼻。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Will, in some percentage of cases, actually make a huge difference to the person's work and time and performance.
zh: Will，在一定比例的案例中，实际上会对这个人的工作、时间和绩效产生巨大的改变。

speaker: Unknown
en: In plenty of cases it doesn't, but that's always where I would start because it so often is just a more fundamental problem that then would lead you to look at other things across the team.
zh: 在很多情况下它不会，但这总是我会开始的地方，因为它通常只是一个更根本的问题，然后会引导你去审视团队中的其他事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, I would say two-way dialogue, but re-clarifying roles and expectations, re-describing the elephant over and over and over again, is one of the hardest parts about being a leader because you feel like a broken record, right?
zh: 但是是的，我会说双向对话，但重新澄清角色和期望，一遍又一遍地重新描述大象，是作为领导者最难的部分之一，因为你觉得像一张坏掉的唱片，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: You feel like an idiot.
zh: 你觉得自己像个白痴。

speaker: Unknown
en: You're like, "I've said this 45 times."
zh: 你会想，“我已经说过 45 次了。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Turns out no one heard you the first 43 and you have to.
zh: 结果发现前 43 次没人听到你说话，而你必须。

speaker: Unknown
en: You have to re-describe it in order for people to hear you and to re-understand their sort of role in what they're doing.
zh: 你必须重新描述它，以便人们听到你并重新理解他们在做的事情中他们的角色。

speaker: Unknown
en: I love how you reframed the way I approached it by starting with, "Here's what I'm seeing.
zh: 我喜欢你重新构建我处理问题的方式，从开始，“这是我看到的。

speaker: Unknown
en: What are you seeing?
zh: 你看到了什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: What do you think your role is? "
zh: 你认为你的角色是什么？”

speaker: Unknown
en: The very non-violent communication oriented, which is a clear pattern on this podcast, just the power of that specific framework.
zh: 这是非常非暴力沟通导向的，这是这个播客上的一个清晰模式，仅仅是那个特定框架的力量。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, totally.
zh: 是的，完全正确。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, like I said, work is about humans and it's...
zh: 嗯，就像我说的，工作是关于人类的，它是……

speaker: Unknown
en: Like I said, work is about humans and it's the art of organizing humans to get something done and build something that's greater than the sum of its parts and that is an art of the humanness in all of us, how do we get people to hear us, how do we get people aligned.
zh: 就像我说过的，工作是关于人类的，它是组织人类去完成某事并建立某种比其部分总和更伟大的东西的艺术，这是我们要所有人的人性艺术，我们如何让人们听到我们，我们如何让人们保持一致。

speaker: Unknown
en: Work for a lifetime.
zh: 这是一辈子的事业。

speaker: Unknown
en: Totally.
zh: 完全同意。

zh: 你是否做出了多捐赠的新年决心？

zh: 我想告诉你 GoFundMe 推出的一个名为 Giving Funds 的新产品，这是一种更智能、更轻松的捐赠方式。
